system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-12-03 13:43:00 to 2179-12-06 12:49:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Crohn’s disease and multiple abdominal surgeries was readmitted three days after discharge for a recent flare, presenting with acute abdominal pain, flank discomfort, and frequent diarrhea. He reported symptom onset after attending a cookout, with stools containing undigested food. Initial concern was for a recurrent Crohn’s flare, but labs showed normal inflammatory markers, and CT imaging revealed improvement in prior ileal wall thickening with no obstruction or abscess. Renal ultrasound ruled out nephrolithiasis. The clinical picture and imaging supported a diagnosis of gastroenteritis, likely viral. The patient was managed with IV fluids, pain control, and dietary advancement from clear liquids. He improved clinically, maintained stable vital signs, and was discharged home on continued prednisone, a low-residue diet, and instructions for follow-up with gastroenterology.
problems: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis
Displacement of lumbar intervertebral disc without myelopathy

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ man with Crohn's disease status post subtotal colectomy
who presents with worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain, looking for
complications of medication or refractory Crohn's disease.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired on a 1.5
Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to, during, and after
the uneventful intravenous administration of 0.1 mmol/kg (15 mL) of
gadolinium-DTPA.  In addition, the patient received 900 mL of VoLumen orally
as an oral contrast agent.  1 mg of glucagon was administered IM to reduce
bowel motion.

COMPARISON:  MRE, ___ and ___.  Also, CT abdomen and
pelvis ___.

MRE:  The patient has had a subtotal colectomy with an ileoanal anastomosis. 
Once again, there is an ~6cm long abnormal thickening of the distal ileum just
proximal to the anastomosis with both mucosal and transmural enhancement
consistent with acute on chronic inflammation.  There is angulation of this
abnormal small bowel seen laterally (11:34), consistent with tethering.  The
appearances are essentially unchanged compared to the prior study of ___.  There is slightly more apparent proximal dilatation of the small bowel
in this region; however, the area of abnormal thickening is widely patent. 
The appearances suggest an acute on chronic stenosing Crohn's disease.  There
is no stranding of the adjacent fat and small lymph nodes seen in the
mesenteric fat (7:17).  There are no additional areas of abnormal enhancement
seen throughout the visualized small bowel, no free fluid seen.

MR ABDOMEN:

Limited images of the liver, spleen, kidneys, and adrenal glands are
unremarkable.  The pancreas is normal.  No upper abdominal lymphadenopathy.

MRI OF THE PELVIS:

The urinary bladder and rectum are unremarkable in appearance.  No free fluid
in the pelvis.  No pelvic lymphadenopathy.  The visualized bone marrow is
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

Approximately 6-cm long segment of abnormally thickened and enhancing distal
ileum just proximal to the level of the ileoanal anastomosis is similar in
appearance compared to multiple prior studies.  There is mild proximal
dilatation of the small bowel at this level; however, the lumen is widely
patent.  The appearances are consistent with acute on chronic stenotic Crohn's
disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in today with worsening left lower abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had this crampy pain in my lower left side for about three days now. It started with more frequent, watery stools—maybe 8 to 10 times a day. That’s not normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had Crohn’s disease for a while, correct? With surgery in the past?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had most of my colon removed years ago. I usually have 3 or 4 bowel movements a day, but this flare felt familiar—until this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until this morning? What changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The diarrhea stopped suddenly. No bowel movement at all. That’s happened before when I ended up with a partial blockage. I got scared and came to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good call. We want to be careful with that. You’re on prednisone right now—15 mg daily—but it’s not helping much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I’ve been on it for weeks, tapering down, but the pain’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve started you on IV fluids, antibiotics—ciprofloxacin—and IV morphine for pain. We’re keeping you NPO for now, meaning nothing by mouth, to let your bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No food? How long will that be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for now. We’re waiting on some tests. Your labs show your white count is slightly elevated, but your inflammatory markers—CRP and sed rate—are actually normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it not a Crohn’s flare then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to say. Given your history, we want to be sure. The GI team recommended an MR enterography to get a detailed look at your small bowel. We’ll schedule that for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to know what’s going on. This pain is exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re here to help. We’ll keep you comfortable and get answers as soon as we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MR enterography was done this morning. I’ve reviewed the results with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a 6-centimeter segment of thickened bowel near your anastomosis—your surgical connection. It’s consistent with chronic Crohn’s inflammation. But here’s the good news: it’s actually improved compared to past scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Improved? But I feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s confusing. The imaging doesn’t show a worsening flare or a blockage. The lumen is widely patent—no obstruction. Your labs also don’t show high inflammation. So we don’t think this is a typical flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why the pain? And why did my bowels stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes, even stable disease can cause symptoms. The sudden stop in bowel movements may have been temporary slowing, not a blockage. We’re going to try advancing your diet today—start with clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see how you do with clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we can move to a full diet tomorrow—no lactose, to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on clear liquids. No nausea or pain with drinking. We’re going to switch you to a full diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I also get something stronger for pain? The morphine helped, but now it’s just occasional Tylenol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. Since we don’t see a clear structural cause for severe pain, we’re avoiding long-term narcotics. We can discuss other options with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been in pain for years. I just need something to get through the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ve involved social work to help connect you with support. They’re concerned you might feel isolated, and we want to make sure you’re not struggling emotionally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve thought about hurting myself, yeah. It’s hard dealing with this all the time. Feels like no one believes me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. That takes courage. We’re setting up a care conference so all your doctors are on the same page—your pain is real, and we want to manage it safely and compassionately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well on a full diet—no lactose. Your labs are improving. White count is down, and your kidney function is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We won’t send you home with narcotics, but we’ll keep your current meds the same—prednisone, loperamide as needed, omeprazole, and B12 shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really wanted something for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But given the lack of a clear cause, we’re concerned about dependency. Instead, GI suggests a lactulose breath test for bacterial overgrowth—could be contributing to symptoms. And maybe a trial of rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. But if the pain gets bad, I’ll go to another ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hope you come back here. We care about you. You have a follow-up with Dr. ___ in the Crohn’s clinic on ___ , and another with your GI doctor on ___ . Please keep those appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved. You’re going home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with the tests and appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send the instructions to your GI team. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to call if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re not alone in this.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Crohn’s disease status post subtotal colectomy was admitted for worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain and increased diarrhea, concerning for a flare. He reported sudden cessation of bowel movements, prompting ED evaluation. Initial labs showed mild leukocytosis but normal inflammatory markers. MR enterography revealed a 6 cm segment of thickened distal ileum, consistent with chronic Crohn’s, but stable or improved compared to prior studies, with no obstruction. The patient was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, antibiotics, and pain control. His diet was advanced successfully, and he tolerated oral intake. Stool studies were negative for infection. He reported passive suicidal ideation and concerns about pain management, prompting social work involvement and a care conference. He was discharged home with unchanged medications and plans for outpatient evaluation of bacterial overgrowth.
